profile.name: Diego Palominos
profile.tagline: I build event-driven systems on AWS and chase vintage guitar tones in my spare time.
profile.credential: Ingeniería de Ejecución en Sistemas Computacionales — UTFSM, Valparaíso · B.Eng. in Computer Systems Engineering

sections.label: Projects
sections.headline: Things I shipped and still stand behind
sections.summary: The systems I wrote and still run or stand behind: a SaaS in production since 2017, a commerce platform whose registers keep selling when the cloud is down, and a control panel that draws its own architecture.

sections.label: Backend
sections.headline: Boring on purpose, fast where it counts
sections.summary: I like backends that are predictable under load and honest about failure. That is how I wrote the modular monolith behind Eleva and the .NET middleware behind Liquor Cart: explicit contracts, idempotent handlers, and an outbox between the database and the message bus.

items.title: A modular monolith in production
items.deck: Eleva: one .NET deployable on PostgreSQL, with module boundaries and tenant scopes enforced in code. New features land as a module, not a rewrite.

items.title: Queues and workers
items.deck: Liquor Cart's middleware, about 90% of its C# mine: services on RabbitMQ with retries, backoff and an error queue an operator can replay. Every consumer is idempotent, because at-least-once always means twice eventually.

items.title: The outbox pattern
items.deck: State change and event publication in one transaction, with an inbox on the other side. The same message twice is a no-op, not a double charge.

sections.label: Frontend
sections.headline: UIs that explain the system underneath
sections.summary: Most of my frontend work is operational: evaluation screens, control panels, storefronts. The goal is always the same — surface state clearly, make actions obvious, and let motion carry meaning instead of decoration.

items.title: Angular, in production
items.deck: Eleva's web app, now on Angular 21: evaluations a whole school answers, one question per screen at a desk or as a conversation on a phone. And a control panel built to be scanned, not read.

items.title: Hyvä storefronts
items.deck: Tailwind-based Magento frontends where performance is a feature. Fewer megabytes, faster paint, happier checkout.

items.title: Motion with intent
items.deck: Transitions that show where things came from and where they went. If an animation does not explain something, it gets cut.

sections.label: Integrations
sections.headline: Third parties fail; integrations shouldn't
sections.summary: Store registers, payment gateways, ERPs — every external system is a distributed-systems problem wearing a vendor logo. I build the seams so they bend instead of break.

items.title: Registers that stay on-premise
items.deck: Liquor Cart's registers never moved to the cloud. Database-level replication carries their data across the boundary, over connections that drop, and the register keeps selling either way.

items.title: Payment gateways
items.deck: Card data stays tokenized at the gateway and every payment action runs under an idempotent key. When money and orders disagree, a sweeper notices before the accountant does.

items.title: Anti-corruption layers
items.deck: The vendor's data model stays at the boundary, behind a small frozen vocabulary of wire events. Inside, the domain speaks its own language and never learns what SOAP is.

sections.label: Event Sourcing
sections.headline: State is a cache; events are the record
sections.summary: Append-only logs, projections you can rebuild, and the quiet confidence of being able to answer 'how did we get here?' for any row in the database.

items.title: Append-only aggregates
items.deck: Liquor Cart's catalog and orders live in an event store: every change is an event with a name, a timestamp, and an author. Current state is just a fold over history.

items.title: Rebuildable projections
items.deck: Read models are disposable by design. This site replays its posts, pages and even its deploys from event one on every boot.

items.title: Schema evolution
items.deck: Events live forever, so they need versioning, upcasting, and a healthy respect for the ones written three years ago.

sections.label: Distributed Systems
sections.headline: Consistency is a spectrum, pick your point
sections.summary: Sagas over two-phase commit, backpressure over wishful thinking, and observability deep enough that 3 a.m. incidents come with a map.

items.title: Sagas and compensation
items.deck: Liquor Cart's payment recovery is a saga with an undo for every ending: void, refund, cancel or complete. When the facts don't resolve, it escalates to a person.

items.title: Backpressure
items.deck: Systems should slow down gracefully instead of falling over heroically. Every store has its own broker virtual host, so one store's retry storm stays in that store.

items.title: Observability
items.deck: OpenTelemetry traces that follow an order from checkout to register, alarms that mean something, and logs you can actually search during an incident.

sections.label: Infrastructure as Code
sections.headline: If it isn't in the repo, it doesn't exist
sections.summary: AWS CDK stacks that build themselves through pipelines, render themselves as diagrams, and shut themselves down when nobody is looking. Infrastructure with a power button.

items.title: CDK everything
items.deck: TypeScript stacks with constructs shaped after the domain, not the console: Eleva, Liquor Cart's Magento and this site. A new environment is a pull request, not a weekend.

items.title: Cost-aware by design
items.deck: Eleva powers down outside school hours on schedule rules, and the application was written to tolerate it. The cheapest instance is the one that is off.

items.title: Pipelines with gates
items.deck: Every stack ships through CodePipeline with manual approval where it matters and automatic rollback where it doesn't. Eleva shipped 129 production releases in 30 days that way.

sections.label: Guitars
sections.headline: Latency zero, uptime whenever I feel like it
sections.summary: Away from the keyboard I collect guitar tones and the colors that come with them: surf green offsets, seafoam Strats, candy apple reds, and sunbursts that fade like a good deploy on a Friday.

items.title: The finishes
items.deck: Fender's custom colors were borrowed from 1950s car paint — Surf Green from Chevrolet, Candy Apple Red mixed over a gold base. Every finish is a story about an era.

items.title: The instruments
items.deck: An offset with a rosewood board for jangle, a humbucker workhorse for weight, and an acoustic dreadnought in three-tone sunburst for the porch.

items.title: The signal chain
items.deck: Tube amps on the edge of breakup, a pedalboard that grows faster than any microservice fleet, and an ongoing argument about whether true bypass matters.

items.title: The collector's bench
items.deck: Nitro finishes, vintage specs, original parts — I collect and sell high-end guitars in Chile, known for listings people can trust. Old guitars are quiet proof that things built with care last.

sections.label: Blog
sections.headline: Writing things down before they bite again
sections.summary: Long-form notes on systems, infrastructure, and the occasional guitar detour. Deployed on ECS, stored cheap, and turned off at night like everything else I run.

items.title: Turning the platform off at night
items.deck: How schedule rules and a control Lambda turned our AWS bill into a lights-out factory, and what broke the first time the lights came back on.

items.title: An outbox is a promise
items.deck: Exactly-once delivery does not exist, but a transactional outbox plus idempotent consumers gets close enough that nobody can tell the difference.

items.title: Surf Green: Fender's happiest accident
items.deck: A short history of the color that started on a 1957 Chevrolet, ended up on offset guitars, and eventually themed this very website.
